mcqs.question: In one stylesheet, :where(.card) a { color: navy; } is written after .card a { color: teal; }. What color do links inside .card get?
options: navy, because the later rule wins
teal, because .card a has higher specificity: :where() contributes zero
navy, because :where() is more specific than a plain class selector
mcqs.explanation: :where() always contributes zero specificity, so its rule counts as just the type selector a, (0,0,1), while .card a is (0,1,1). Specificity is compared before source order, so teal wins even though navy is declared later. The strongest distractor is option 0: 'last one wins' only applies when specificity ties, and opting out of the specificity fight is the entire point of :where().

mcqs.question: A desktop media query uses grid-template-areas to display region C first, then A and B, but the DOM order is A, B, C. What do keyboard users and screen-reader reading order follow?
options: The visual order produced by the grid placement
The order the areas are named in grid-template-areas
Keyboard users follow the visual order, but screen readers follow the DOM order
mcqs.explanation: CSS visual reordering never changes the underlying DOM order, and both sequential keyboard navigation and screen-reader reading follow source order, so those users encounter A, B, C while sighted users see C first. The fix is to correct the HTML source order and keep CSS purely presentational. The strongest distractor is option 3: it sounds like a reasonable split, but there is no split; both channels follow the document, which is exactly why the mismatch is disorienting.

mcqs.question: With @layer base, components; declared, a rule in @layer components sets a property, and a later unlayered author rule sets the same property with lower specificity. Which declaration wins?
options: The layered rule, because it was declared first
The layered rule, because layers outrank unlayered styles
The unlayered rule, because unlayered author styles take precedence over layered ones for normal declarations
Whichever rule appears later in the file
mcqs.explanation: For normal declarations from the same origin, the cascade compares cascade layers before specificity, and unlayered author styles rank above all layered author styles; that is exactly what makes unlayered utilities a deliberate override strategy (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer). The strongest distractor is option 1: the intuition that layers are the strong tier is backwards for normal declarations, and importance flips the order rather than reinforcing it. Option 3 fails because source order only decides within the same layer and specificity tier.

scenarios.prompt: For the CSS below, determine the final color of the link in each of the three cases, and justify each result by walking the cascade in the correct order.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Case 1: orange. The inline style is an author-origin normal declaration that outranks every other author normal declaration, regardless of layer or specificity. Case 2: purple. For normal declarations from the same origin, the cascade compares cascade layers before specificity, and unlayered author styles rank above all layered author styles, so the unlayered rule beats both layered ones without any specificity comparison. Case 3: green. With the unlayered rule gone, layer order decides: components was declared after base, so the components rule wins; note that the :where() in base contributing zero specificity is irrelevant here, because the layer comparison happens before specificity is even consulted. The general walkthrough order is: origin and importance, then cascade layer, then specificity (where :where() counts as zero and :is(), :not(), and :has() take their most specific argument), then source order, with scoping proximity before order where it applies. The classic error is jumping straight to 'last rule in the file wins', which only holds inside a single layer at equal specificity.
rubric: Gets all three colors right: orange, purple, green.
Walks the cascade in order: origin and importance, then layer, then specificity, then source order.
Knows unlayered author styles outrank layered ones for normal declarations.
Knows an inline style beats other author normal declarations regardless of layer or specificity.
Can say when :where()'s zero specificity matters (same layer) and when it is preempted (layer comparison first).
